name: Carb cycling / refeeds
lead: Carb cycling alternates higher-carbohydrate and lower-carbohydrate days, often timed around training; the higher days are often called refeeds. Protein usually stays roughly constant while fat is adjusted in the opposite direction to carbohydrate [1]. People use it to get leaner while holding on to muscle and to keep training quality up, which shows in a more defined, muscular physique.

Proponents say refeeds replenish muscle glycogen for harder sessions, ease the psychological load of dieting and may offset some of the metabolic slowdown that accompanies weight loss [1][2]. Review authors describe planned refeeds and diet breaks as one strategy for metabolic adaptation, and physique-athlete guidelines list them as possibly beneficial during contest preparation [2][3][4].

Trials so far compare intermittent dieting with continuous dieting rather than carb cycling by name. A 2025 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials found similar fat loss in both approaches, with resting metabolic rate falling significantly only after continuous restriction [5].

paras: A common weekly pattern is described as two to four higher-carbohydrate days and three to five lower-carbohydrate days. Refeeds are higher-carbohydrate days or intermittent diet breaks within a calorie deficit [1].

Researchers use the umbrella term intermittent energy restriction for alternating periods of restriction with periods of greater intake, called refeeds or diet breaks, and contrast it with continuous energy restriction [2].

Grokipedia attributes carb cycling to late-1980s bodybuilding and to Franco Carlotto, though that attribution rests on popular fitness websites rather than primary research. It spread through flexible dieting and online fitness communities in the 2010s and 2020s [1].

Proponents claim fat loss with muscle retention, better training-day performance from glycogen replenishment, improved metabolic flexibility and easier adherence. Some propose that refeeds partly restore leptin and thyroid-related hormones; glycogen restoration also raises scale weight temporarily through water retention [1].

A 2019 review proposes that periods of energy balance during restriction may attenuate some of the adaptive responses that resist continued fat loss, while noting that evidence of effectiveness in athletic populations is lacking [2].

A 2022 review of metabolic adaptation lists increased protein, high-fibre foods, planned refeeds and diet breaks among strategies to confront the body's drive to regain lost mass [3]. A 2020 review of nutrition for physique athletes recommends slower weight loss of up to 0.5% of body mass per week and says diet breaks and refeeds are possibly beneficial [4].

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials with 881 participants found improvements in body mass, fat mass and waist circumference after both intermittent dieting with breaks and continuous restriction, without significant group differences; resting metabolic rate fell significantly only after continuous restriction [5]. A 2026 randomized trial in 30 women with obesity compared 12 weeks of continuous restriction with structured refeeds and diet breaks; body fat percentage fell by 6.7% in the continuous group and 6.0% in the refeed group [6]. The BREAK trial protocol is testing intermittent restriction against continuous restriction for adaptive thermogenesis [7].

Per Grokipedia, one trial of intermittent restriction with refeeds in resistance-trained people reported less fat-free mass loss than continuous restriction, and authors note that benefits may stem from calorie cycling rather than carbohydrate alternation [1].

Reported downsides include fatigue, irritability and gastrointestinal upset in low-carbohydrate phases, overeating on high-carbohydrate days, and possible disordered eating tied to rigid rules. Clinical advice cited includes consulting a professional with diabetes, thyroid disorders, eating disorder history or pregnancy [1].

Trials have compared intermittent dieting with refeeds or diet breaks against continuous restriction, mostly in people with overweight or obesity, and have not tested carb cycling by name for appearance outcomes [5][6]. The 2025 meta-analysis found similar fat loss in both approaches and a smaller drop in resting metabolic rate with breaks [5].

lore.intro: Lifters on T Nation discuss refeeds and cyclical or targeted low-carbohydrate eating as tools for getting lean while keeping training performance.

claims.claim: Periodic carb refeeds keep thyroid function and glycogen up so fat loss continues with less muscle loss
claims.believers: One T Nation poster describing a very-low-calorie protocol says a carb refeed every few days keeps the thyroid going and glycogen full to maximise fat loss and minimise muscle loss [8].
claims.experts: Reviews describe refeeds as a proposed way to blunt metabolic adaptation, but note evidence in athletes is lacking, and a meta-analysis found similar fat loss with and without breaks [2][5].

claims.claim: Targeted or cyclical keto with refeed days keeps you lean without constant hunger
claims.believers: A T Nation user reports months of targeted keto with refeed days, staying lean without crazy hunger [9].
claims.experts: No trials were found of cyclical ketogenic diets by name in the cited literature; related work compares intermittent and continuous calorie restriction [5].

card.summary: Alternating high- and low-carb days to lean out; direct evidence is thin and fat loss tracks total calories.
card.note: Source base is a single AI-generated encyclopedia page; treat details cautiously.

quick.overview:
Carb cycling swaps higher- and lower-carbohydrate days, with high days called refeeds. It comes from bodybuilding and flexible dieting.

Believers say it keeps muscle and eases dieting. Direct research is limited.
quick.mechanism: Higher-carb days are proposed to restore glycogen, hunger hormones and training performance. Overall calorie deficit is described as the main driver of fat loss.
quick.risks: Possible fatigue in low-carb phases, overeating on high-carb days, and disordered eating in some people.

chain: Higher-carbohydrate days replenish glycogen and break up the deficit
Training quality and diet adherence are supported
More muscle kept while body fat falls, giving a leaner physique
angle.text: Carb cycling is used during fat loss so that training stays strong and the diet stays sustainable, with the aim of keeping muscle while losing fat. Physique athletes and online lifters use it as a way to get leaner while looking full [1][4].
